item.title: Flatness-based control of nonlinear complex networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.37436v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective control of nonlinear complex networks needs to identify not only the intervention sites but also the state variables to be monitored and the locations at which control inputs should be applied. Here, we present a network-scale generalization of an observability-guided, flatness-based control framework. The resulting control laws are implemented using sliding-mode control and evaluated in heterogeneous networks of chaotic oscillators driven toward a prescribed periodic regime. We compare two control architectures: in the node-wise method, oscillators are independently sensed and actuated, while in the pairwise method, measurements acquired from a single node within each dyad are used to synthesize control inputs applied to both nodes. Across the parameter regimes considered, node-wise control generally achieves accurate control over a broader operating region, whereas pairwise control remains effective over a more restricted region while using half as many measurement locations for a given number of actuated nodes. Moreover, network interactions can enhance control by propagating the control influence to non-actuated nodes, creating a cooperative effect between the collective dynamics and the control action. Collectively, these findings quantify the trade-offs among measurement-location requirements, control performance, and control effort in nonlinear complex networks.
item.dc:creator: I. Sendi\~na-Nadal, I. Leyva, J. P. Barbot, C. Letellier

item.title: Cutting, Shuffling and Diffusion as a Coarsening Process
item.description: arXiv:2610.35979v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cutting and shuffling (CS) rearranges fluid without stretching, but homogenisation requires diffusion (D); this interaction is not well understood. We show that CSD is a coarsening process, with scale $\bar\ell=L(n_c\mathrm{Pe}/2)^{-1/3}$ rather than the Batchelor scale, and that cutting acts as a fractional Laplacian in wavenumber, giving the exact mixing rate $\gamma=2^{1/3}|a_1'|n_c^{2/3}\lambda\mathrm{Pe}^{-1/3}$ for $n_c$ cuts per event at rate $\lambda$, with $a_1'=-1.0188\dots$ the first zero of $\mathrm{Ai}'$. This holds in any dimension for random and deterministic protocols, extends to finite-time mixing, and places CSD in a known non-equilibrium universality class.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Lester, Tanguy LeBorgne, Joris Heyman

item.title: Exploring Neural Dynamics with Time Delays: A Numerical and Bifurcation Analysis Approach
item.description: arXiv:2610.36920v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Wilson-Cowan model is a classic example of a ``neural mass model'' - a simplified yet powerful way to describe the activity of large networks of neurons. It is particularly interesting because, even in its relatively simple form, it can produce a surprising variety of behaviours, from steady rhythms to complex oscillations. A key factor influencing these dynamics is the presence of time delays, reflecting the time it takes for signals to travel between neurons. This article offers an accessible introduction to the Wilson-Cowan model, focusing on how these time delays affect its behaviour. We explore the core concepts behind the model, survey the existing literature, and introduce some numerical techniques specifically designed for analysing such delay differential equations. We also provide a practical, hands-on tutorial on using the DDE-BIFTOOL software package, demonstrating its application to the Wilson-Cowan model. Downloadable code allows the reader to reproduce our results and to explore the model's dynamics further, including MATLAB code for all computations, using DDE-BIFTOOL for the continuation, and Python versions of simulation codes.
item.dc:creator: Martin R Nelson, Jonathan J Crofts

item.title: Another Brick in the Wall: Spectral Form Factor of Normal Modes in Horizonless Geometries
item.description: arXiv:2610.37038v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We compute the normal mode spectrum and its spectral form factor for a probe scalar wave in smooth horizonless backgrounds. We first consider the BTZ black hole with a brickwall that hides the near-horizon region, which has recently been proposed as a toy model for a finite-temperature semiclassical black hole microstate. In this setup, the spectral form factor may or may not have a linear ramp, depending on the details of the brickwall construction. However, we argue that even in cases that do show a ramp, this ramp does not originate from level correlations associated with quantum chaos. Then we calculate the normal mode spectrum for a genuine microstate geometry (superstratum) and find evidence of chaos, both with a ramp and level repulsion. We conclude that the eigenvalue spectrum of normal modes can indeed serve as a tool for investigating the quantum dynamics of fuzzballs; however, the brickwall models are incapable of capturing this phenomenon.
item.dc:creator: A. I. Belokon, M. \v{C}ubrovi\'c, V. {\DJ}uki\'c, V. V. Pushkarev, L. Umrikhin

item.title: Transport statistics in asymmetric coupled chaotic dots in series: Brownian motion model
item.description: arXiv:2610.37090v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study statistics of transport properties in a system of two quantum chaotic cavities coupled in series through a tunable junction and connected to reservoirs with asymmetric leads. Within the random matrix theory framework and in the absence of time-reversal symmetry, the scattering matrix S undergoes a crossover from two independent circular unitary ensembles to a single CUE as the inter-cavity coupling increases. Modeling this crossover using Dyson's Brownian motion approach, with the junction width acting as a time-like parameter, we derive closed-form expressions for the time-dependent averages and variances of conductance and shot noise power for arbitrary lead asymmetry. These analytical results reduce to known expressions in the symmetric and fully coupled limits. The mapping between the Brownian time parameter and the physical junction width is found to be observable-dependent, reflecting the different eigenfunction correlations probed by conductance and shot noise power, and this dependence is examined and separately calibrated for each observable. Validating against random-matrix simulations and tight-binding transport calculations using Kwant, we find quantitative agreement for ensemble-averaged observables throughout the crossover, while variances, being more sensitive to microscopic fluctuations, show deviations from the Brownian-motion predictions.
item.dc:creator: Ashutosh Dheer, Santosh Kumar, Jayendra N. Bandyopadhyay

item.title: Hamiltonian Chaos
item.description: arXiv:2604.12976v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Through semiclassical methods the subject of quantum chaos motivates and depends on Hamiltonian chaos research. Presented here is a selection of some of the most important Hamiltonian chaos topics that in this way get directly related to any of a variety of quantum chaos research problems. The overall emphasis is on intuitive explanations and illustrations of various ideas with the references containing more mathematically rigorous expositions. The chapter begins with a description of various useful theoretical and computational tools of chaos research, e.g.~surfaces of section, paradigms of chaos, stability analysis, and symbolic dynamics... This is followed by discussions regarding the geometry of chaos, how chaotic systems respond to perturbations, and the complexification of Hamiltonian dynamics. Most of the contents concern topics that are long established and well known by now. The exceptions involve complications that arise from the complexification of phase space variables and time. There are relatively recent results summarized regarding the appropriate branches of determinant phases and how to distinguish complex trajectories that are associated with classically allowed processes versus those associated with non-allowed ones.
item.dc:creator: Steven Tomsovic
